title: His son's cancer and death in Silver Spring
summary: The son, a health-conscious engineer, is found to have cancer of the lung and liver and dies within weeks; Tate carries on playing in Europe.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: So he was jogging, he ran down under the hill and he told me he was completely exhausted when he got down to the bottom of that hill. He couldn't get back up. He told me he

had to crawl back up the hill. So his wife rushed him to the hospital and you know, when they rushed him to the hospital this time, they found cancer in the lung and the liver. Two weeks and a half after the last examination, just that quick.

So I knew -- when they told me that, I knew he wasn't going to make it. But he was brave all the way. And he stayed strong, you know, like for a long time. Even the day when he died, he died in my sister's arms, and I went there, but he always said, 'Dad, don't worry about me.' He says, 'This is a bad thing I got,' he says, 'people hardly beat the liver, but I'm going to beat it.' He says, 'I know. I feel like I'm going to beat it and I know I'm going to beat it.' I think the medicine was really too strong for him and they wanted to change it and the medicine that they were going to change him to, they had to -- if he wasn't able to stand it, it would have killed him one dose. So they had to open him up to see if he was able to take it and when they opened him up, they found out he would have been able to take it. And after that, he just started to --

Yeah, just started to decline. So the day he died, he told my sister, says, 'Aunt Daisy, I thought I could beat this, but I can't beat it.' He says, 'But I don't want you all to worry because I've accepted it.' He said, 'It was very hard,' says, 'I hate to leave my little boys.

They won't even know they had a dad," he says, "but that's what's worrying me more than anything else. But don't you all worry," he says, "because I'm ready." And didn't even go in a coma, just closed his eyes and died. So that kind of got to me, you know, it really shook me up. And I guess when I went over there, there was so many -- some of those -- you know, sometimes I would start at the festival like at 12:00 and maybe do one show and the festival would go like to 12:00, you know, at night, from 12 to 12, you know. I went home one night, first night in London -- this was in London -- and I closed that door and I couldn't stand that house. I had to come out of there. So then I would stay -- like if I finished at 12:00, I'd stay there until 10:30, 12:00, and come home with some of the guys, you know, because it kept it off my mind, you know, when I would be with some of the musicians. It didn't bother me like it would when I'd go home.
